text: Perfect. Just give me a second here. Okay. So once again, welcome. Thank you folks for inviting us back here once again this year. It's always good to see all of you, Reeve and Jeff and missing Ian, of course, and Karen and Claus. We just also appreciate the opportunity to just share with the residents of Montague Township watching on the live stream, just what we've been up to this past year and give you a quick update. So the first one that I would mention is just off of our slide, the really big accomplishment that we were able to do this year is our website is up and running now. And it's completely live. If you get an opportunity to go and check it out, we'd strongly encourage you to do so. And it's right there on our opening slide of www.rulefasd.ca. And it'll give you an update in terms of all the different programs and events and everything that we've been up to over the past couple of years. Just in terms of background, we are still at this point a nonprofit corporation. We have began the process to get our charity status, however, but as anything with the CRA, that is not a quick process. So it's hard to say exactly when that will be done. Our organization does continue to consist solely of people with lived experience dealing with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. This past year, we have experienced significant growth. Once again, we have gone from 121 families to 156 families now in the past 12 months, including we're now up to three families from Montague Township, including my own. Things remain the same from a social service standpoint, from a governmental support standpoint, the current MCCSS criteria still does not recognize FASD as a eligible disability under passport funding, as well as SSAH. And so we continue to advocate at the provincial level to see that change. It should be noted as well that research has demonstrated that 4% of our population at this point are living with this disability compared to the 1.5% living with autism and the 0.6% living with intellectual disabilities, which are the current eligible criteria. Research has also demonstrated that 90% of children with FASD are going to have mental health challenges. And we within our group have certainly seen that in combination with COVID. It's been a tough year. That's all I'm gonna say there. And we also know from research that 75% of their caregivers are going to have a mental health breakdown at some point in their lifetime. This is why we have really prioritized within our organization that mental health and wellbeing support. And so through our Bell Let's Talk grant, we have been able to pay out almost $16,000 in this past year to help with private counseling for youth with FASD, as well as caregivers getting certified as Mental Health First Aiders. What a Mental Health First Aider is, is it's basically a support individual who can initially recognize when someone's mental health is starting to deteriorate. They do not provide the counseling aspect. That's why it's considered a First Aider. It's the initial recognition that mental health is starting to break down. And so we were able to pay for almost 35 caregivers to receive that training. And we've certainly seen the benefit of that over this past year in doing so. We've also been able to provide system navigation, as well as peer facilitated for support for caregivers, as well as peer mentoring for children and youth with FASD. And I think that's probably what I'm most proud of. And I'm gonna speak to that a little bit later when we get to our financials. But we are very much, the peer facilitated one-on-one support is we have, we've been able to hire eight youth from Lanark County who basically work one-on-one with a youth with FASD and kind of work with them in terms of life skills, work with them from a friendship and social engagement standpoint and so on. Very similar to the things that you've seen Big Brothers do in the past, but the eight individuals that we've been able to hire, they all received specific training on characteristics associated with FASD and best practice strategies on how to support those individuals. In terms of our governance, that's been the other aspect that has really changed and what we've focused on this past year. We're thrilled to be able to announce at this point that we have entered into a formal memorandum of understanding with open doors for Lanark children and youth, and they are serving as our organizational mentor for our board of directors. And we're currently going through some changes related to that. We just had our AGM this past month, and we are pleased to announce that once again, we have all 10 director positions filled, including one who is actually living with FASD to give that first-person perspective on all the decision-making that we're doing at an organizational level. The third aspect that we've done is through a grant from the Ontario Brain Institute, we were able to hire a program evaluator who basically went through our entire organization and laid out the blueprint as to exactly who we are and what we do. That document is coming out shortly, but what we have done is we've identified the four main pillars of service that we're providing. And the four main pillars, number one is education awareness, second is fellowship, and I'm gonna speak to that a little bit later, third is support, and then the last one is the skill-building aspect. What is really fascinating though from that program evaluation is we have been told that from a grassroots organization, which we are, for us to be able to go from a seed to now a scale status in four years is shocking. It's not something that you see very often. And so we, through that, have been able to identify what is it that we're doing from a rural accessibility standpoint, what is it that we're doing that's creating so much engagement? What is it that we're doing that's creating so much growth? And we've identified it really is those four pillars, and in particular, it's the fellowship piece. The last aspect is in terms of governance, our AGM is every February, our minutes, financials, everything are completely open to the public and can be located, once again, on our website, and we invite anyone to go and take a look at that. The last one that I wanted to mention is we are also conducting the first environmental scan of FASD-informed services in Ontario, and we are still on schedule for that gap analysis report to be posted in May in just a couple months. We are, in fact, the individual that is producing the report and I, we pretty much have the rough draft done now. We're kind of just starting to put the final touches in terms of the final draft and so on together. This is gonna be humongous because we've already been told that as long as Minister Clark is reelected come the June election, he will absolutely be bringing this report forward to Queen's Park with our support. The other thing that it does, though, that I think that we're so excited about is through this report, I don't know if you're aware of this, but there are 12 sectors that all of us deal with within our lives, that everything in terms of our engagement, everything that we need within a community standpoint, it can all be put into 12 sectors. And through this report, we've been able to interview over 85 different organizations within the counties of Lanarkin, Leeds, Grenville. We have all of their contact information. We have a description of all the different services that they do. And it's all gonna be put into that one document and then shared back out to all of those different organizations. And we see this as being so key because there's so many times when organizations are working in isolation and in silos, and they don't know if they're having to deal with a different sector. For example, what does the hospital know about recreation opportunities in a municipality? Likely don't. And so this report is gonna be able to connect all those different organizations and all those different sectors together so that everyone has that common information. And we really see this as a really great community building opportunity going forward.
